note: WHO DECIDES WHAT: the one declaration of the boundary between the deterministic rule layer
(packages/judge/src/rules.ts) and the trained scorer's per-subtype heads.
It is a FILE, and language-neutral, because two programs need this same fact and they are not
written in the same language: score-rules.ts gates the rule layer against real captures, and
train-screenreader-model.py decides which heads may block a release. It was declared twice -- a
TypeScript array and a Python frozenset -- and by the time anyone compared them they had already
drifted apart in BOTH directions:
- the TypeScript list carried `4.1.2:unnamed-form-field`, a key that exists in no record
- the Python set omitted the 115 unnamed-form-field records entirely, because it keyed on the
corpus vocabulary and the TypeScript keyed on a criterion it minted itself
Secure by Design 12.5 names this exactly: DRY is about duplicated KNOWLEDGE, not duplicated text.
Two encodings of one business rule 'evolve inconsistently', and the duplication is invisible to a
text-duplication tool because the two encodings do not look alike. That is what happened here.
## The key is the corpus's own subtype vocabulary
`target.subtypes` in the dataset export -- `1.1.1:missing-alt`, `4.1.2:regex` -- and NOT
`provenance.subtype`, which is a case-family name and is ambiguous: `regex` is three different
subtypes under 2.4.4, 2.4.6 and 4.1.2. The model's heads are named after this vocabulary and the
scorer report keys on it, so making the rule gate speak it too means one vocabulary, not two.
## `reportsAs` exists because the two layers disagree, defensibly
The corpus labels an unnamed form field `3.3.2:unnamed-form-field` (a missing label); the rule
reports it under 4.1.2 (a missing accessible name). Both are correct readings of the same page.
Declaring the mapping is the only way the gate can check the rule fired at all -- and previously
this fact lived in a Python comment that the TypeScript side could not see, which is why the
TypeScript side invented a key for it.
## Absence means the model decides it
Only the exceptions are listed. A subtype missing from this file is the scorer's, and the gate
asserts the rules never fire its criterion on it -- so a new subtype the rules DO touch fails
loudly rather than being silently adopted.

1.1.1:filename-alt.note: An exact-absence case: alt text that is a filename is no alternative at all.

1.1.1:missing-alt.note: An exact-absence case. NVDA's 'unlabeled' prefix is nondeterministic, and keying on it once cost 3 of 88 -- the defect that made this gate exist.

3.3.2:unnamed-form-field.note: See `reportsAs` above: the corpus calls it a missing label, the rule calls it a missing accessible name. These records also carry `4.1.2:missing-role`, so the gate must credit that subtype for them too or its boundary reads as ragged.

4.1.2:regex.note: An exact-absence case: a control announced with a role and no name.

note: The rules cover a deliberate SUBSET and the scorer's head owns the rest, so neither 'rules' nor
silence is true. VAGUE_LINK_NAMES is six phrases chosen to be the ones context cannot rescue;
the corpus generates its link text from a wider vocabulary, so the rules fire on part of it.
This was invisible before: the old gate filtered to the two criteria it already believed the
rules owned, so a rule firing on any OTHER criterion could not be seen at all. Declaring the
overlap is what makes it visible; the gate asserts it stays a strict, non-empty subset, so
widening the vocabulary to everything (or breaking the rule to nothing) both fail.
